name: Balanitis xerotica obliterans (genital lichen sclerosus)
aliases: lichen sclerosus et atrophicus of the penis

reference.source: Campbell-Walsh-Wein Urology / WHO laboratory manual for semen analysis
clinicalPearls: Balanitis xerotica obliterans is the genital form of lichen sclerosus in men, producing white, atrophic, scarring change of the glans and prepuce
It characteristically affects the foreskin and glans and may extend to the meatus, causing a firm white sclerotic ring, phimosis, and meatal narrowing
Presenting features include a non-retractile foreskin, painful erections, splitting or bleeding of the prepuce, and a poor or deflected urinary stream from meatal stenosis
Meatal and urethral involvement can lead to stricture disease and obstructed voiding, so the urethra should always be assessed
It is a chronic inflammatory dermatosis rather than an infection, and topical high-potency corticosteroid is the mainstay of medical treatment
Circumcision is frequently both diagnostic and therapeutic and often resolves preputial disease, while meatal or urethral involvement may require reconstructive surgery
There is a recognised, if uncommon, association with penile squamous cell carcinoma, so persistent, atypical, or non-healing lesions should be biopsied and lesions kept under review
Histological confirmation is advisable in doubtful cases and mandatory where malignancy is suspected
reference.pathophysiology: Balanitis xerotica obliterans is a chronic lymphocyte-mediated inflammatory dermatosis of the genital skin, regarded as the male genital manifestation of lichen sclerosus. Immune-mediated inflammation in the dermis drives hyalinisation and homogenisation of the upper dermal collagen with epidermal atrophy, producing the characteristic pale, sclerotic, and fragile tissue. Chronic scarring contracts the prepuce to cause acquired phimosis and narrows the external meatus, and progressive fibrosis may extend proximally into the anterior urethra to produce strictures. The persistent inflammation and epithelial change are believed to underlie the small but definite increase in risk of penile squamous cell carcinoma associated with long-standing disease. The cause is incompletely understood, with genetic, autoimmune, and local factors, including chronic exposure to urine under an unretractable foreskin, all implicated.
additionalDifferentials: Non-specific or infective balanitis, including candidal balanitis
Psoriasis or lichen planus of the genitalia
Penile intraepithelial neoplasia or invasive squamous cell carcinoma
additionalInvestigations: Clinical inspection of the glans, prepuce, and meatus with assessment of foreskin retractility
Assessment of the urinary stream and, where obstruction is suspected, uroflowmetry
Biopsy of atypical, persistent, or non-healing lesions to confirm the diagnosis and exclude malignancy
Urethral imaging or endoscopy where meatal or urethral stricture is suspected
Swab or microscopy to exclude coexistent candidal or bacterial infection
Blood glucose testing, as poorly controlled diabetes predisposes to balanitis
redFlags: A persistent ulcer, indurated plaque, or exophytic lesion suggesting penile squamous cell carcinoma
Progressive meatal stenosis or urethral stricture causing obstructed voiding or retention
New nodularity or bleeding within an established plaque
reference.prognosis: Most preputial disease is controlled by topical corticosteroid or cured by circumcision, but meatal and urethral involvement can be recurrent and may need reconstructive surgery, and lifelong awareness of the small malignant potential warrants ongoing surveillance of persistent lesions.
pitfalls: Treating recurrent balanitis symptomatically without recognising underlying lichen sclerosus
Overlooking meatal and urethral involvement and the resulting stricture disease
Failing to biopsy a suspicious or non-healing lesion and missing an early carcinoma
Assuming circumcision alone always cures disease that has extended to the meatus or urethra
Neglecting long-term follow-up given the malignant association
references: British Association of Dermatologists guidance on lichen sclerosus
European Association of Urology guidance on penile disease
management: First-line medical treatment with a high-potency topical corticosteroid applied to the affected glans and prepuce
Circumcision for corticosteroid-refractory preputial disease or phimosis, which is often both diagnostic and curative
Treat meatal or urethral stricture disease with meatotomy, meatoplasty or urethral reconstruction as required
Use emollients, treat any coexisting candidal or bacterial infection, and optimise glycaemic control in diabetes
Biopsy persistent, atypical or non-healing lesions to exclude penile squamous cell carcinoma
Provide long-term surveillance of persistent lesions given the small but definite malignant potential
Refer to urology or andrology for surgical assessment and to dermatology for refractory dermatosis
